metadata.title: What Else Did You Run?
metadata.topic: COMPUTATIONAL SKEPTICISM · HOW TO LIE WITH DATA

beats.narration_text: Most people picture data manipulation as making numbers up. That's the rare version, and it's the one that gets caught. This is Sai. I wrote a post that does the common version instead: one synthetic dataset where I know the true answer, twelve standard analytical tricks, and two press releases that reach opposite conclusions. Every number in both of them is real.

show.event: the composer opens on the greeting and the topic chip
the ask types in — build the dataset with a known answer, then run the playbook against it
the first result line lands: one dataset, twelve thousand residents, a true effect of fourteen hundred a year

the third lands: one chart that recovers the truth

props.command: I generated twelve thousand residents and built in a job-training effect of exactly fourteen hundred dollars a year, so I know the ground truth. Now run the standard analytical playbook against it — pick the rows, the window, the denominator, the average, the axis — and show me how far from fourteen hundred a defensible analysis can land without ever printing a false number.
output: two press releases, opposite conclusions, zero fabricated numbers
one chart that recovers the truth — the specification curve

beats.narration_text: I wrote the data-generating process myself, so the true effect is exactly fourteen hundred dollars a year, the same for everyone. Every other number on this axis is also real, computed from the same twelve thousand rows. They run from about eleven hundred dollars to nearly eight thousand, and two of them point in opposite directions.

the band settles: where every analysis that accounts for selection lands
the district cherry-pick arrives low on the scale
the true effect lands in terracotta, inside the band — the one figure that was built by hand
the pre-registered estimate lands beside it
the subgroup claim jumps a decade out
both press-release claims land furthest right, far past the truth

data.slideMeta: SAME 12,000 ROWS · SIZE OF EACH PUBLISHED CLAIM, SIGN SET ASIDE

beats.narration_text: Same twelve thousand rows. The program office says graduates out-earn everyone else by seven thousand nine hundred and eighty-eight dollars. The opposition says participants fall five thousand six hundred and forty-seven behind. Both are computed correctly. Both are publishable. The truth is fourteen hundred, and neither side is anywhere near it.

show.event: one dataset sits at the start of the track, with one true answer inside it
the split opens on the only question that mattered — which conclusion did you want
the upper track climbs: the program office packet, three real statistics
the lower track falls: the taxpayers alliance packet, three more real statistics
both endpoints hold on screen at once — irreconcilable, and drawn from the same rows

data.slideMeta: THE NARRATIVE MACHINE · CONCLUSION IN, EVIDENCE OUT

beats.narration_text: One choice sits underneath all of it. People don't enrol at random. The program recruits hardest where need is greatest, so participants start out poorer before it does anything at all. Ignore that, and your estimate lands anywhere from minus six thousand to plus eight thousand. Account for it, and every version lands near fifteen hundred.

show.event: the question sets the fork: does your comparison account for who chose to enrol
the naive branch opens — compare whoever showed up, as measured
its consequence lands: an estimate that spans both sides of zero
the second branch opens — account for the selection mechanism
its consequence lands: every version inside a few hundred dollars
the resolver settles under both — the problem is the comparison, not the sample size

beats.narration_text: None of this needs a bad person. It's what happens when someone with a preferred conclusion gets to make analytic choices after seeing the data. Which rows. Which window. Which denominator. Which average. Where the axis starts. Each one has a justification you could say out loud in a meeting.

the first pair lands: which rows, which window
the second pair lands: which denominator, which average
the last pair completes the grid: where the axis goes, which comparison gets published
the caption settles — each has a justification you could say out loud

props.sparkLine: Twelve tricks. Not one of them alters a number.

props.caption: Stacked together, they reach almost any conclusion you decided on in advance.

beats.narration_text: The antidote is about twenty lines of code: run every defensible analysis and plot all of them. The ones that ignore selection scatter across both sides of zero. The ones that account for it cluster within a few hundred dollars of the truth. Then quoting only the flattering one needs an explanation.

show.event: the artifact page opens on the title
the first line lands: twelve analyses, the naive ones spanning both sides of zero
the second lands: the selection-aware cluster, and the true effect inside the interval
the third lands: the fix is procedural, not moral
the fourth settles the page — all twelve on one chart changes what an analyst can quietly omit

props.artifactHeading: How to lie with data · one page
artifactLines: Twelve defensible analyses of the same twelve thousand people. The ones that ignore who chose to enrol scatter from -$6,355 to +$7,988, on both sides of zero. Any one of them, presented alone with its methods paragraph, is publishable.
The ones that account for selection cluster between $1,496 and $1,963. The pre-registered estimate is $1,817, with a 95% interval from $1,379 to $2,255. The true effect, $1,400, sits inside it.
The spread among the naive analyses is not a measurement problem. Ten times as many rows would give you the same wrong answers with tighter confidence intervals.
The defenses are procedural, not moral. Write the analysis plan before you see the outcomes. Report the whole specification curve, not the specification you liked.

beats.narration_text: Here's yours. Take one chart you actually read this week and ask it three things. Who is in each group, and how did they get there. What happened to everyone who dropped out. How many analyses were run before this one. What you can't answer from the page is the finding.

show.event: the composer returns on "Your turn."
the prompt types in — bring a real chart, not a hypothetical one
the three questions land inside the ask
the running line settles — what you can't answer is the finding

props.command: Take one chart from a dashboard, an earnings deck, or a news article I actually read this week. Run these three against it: who is in each group and how did they get there, what happened to everyone who dropped out, and how many analyses were run before this one. Then tell me which of the three I cannot answer from what is on the page.

beats.narration_text: A number is a claim about a procedure. What was measured, who was included, what was tried first. Numbers don't lie. The procedure does, and it's usually the part that isn't shown. This is Sai.

the handle settles beneath it
the subline closes the page
